```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "yu2021")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/08_yu2021_spectral_mait.R first. ",
      "See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}

measures <- ReadOutput("sample_measures.csv")
verdicts <- ReadOutput("claim_verdicts.csv")
```

## Why this dataset

The OMIP-039 and OMIP-043 reports both worked on one panel at a time, on a
conventional analyser, and they asked whether an automated method lands where an
expert lands. Neither of them left the conventional instrument.

A spectral analyser is a different machine. It does not assign one detector to
one fluorochrome. It records the emission of every fluorochrome across 64
detectors and then solves for the contribution of each one, which is why a
spectral panel carries 35 markers where a conventional panel carries 20.

This report uses FlowRepository FR-FCM-Z3WR, which is the flow cytometry deposit
of Yu and colleagues [1]. The paper reports that circulating mucosal-associated
invariant T cells fall in COVID-19, and that the fall is larger in females. The
files are Cytek Aurora, the panel is 35 named markers, and the deposit holds 83
samples from 45 subjects.

The dataset was chosen because the claim can be tested. The paper states ten
findings that rest on the flow data alone, and Table S1 of the paper carries the
sex, the severity rank, the time point and the seroconversion status of every
sample. The claims live in `gating/yu2021_paper_claims.csv` with the sentence
each one came from, so a reader can check the claim against the paper before
checking the number against the data.

```{r}
#| label: panel

panel <- ReadOutput("panel.csv")
named <- panel[panel$is_marker == TRUE, ]
kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = c("Parameters in the file", "Named markers",
                "Unnamed fluorescence channels", "Scatter and time channels",
                "Samples", "Subjects", "Median events per sample"),
    Value = c(
      nrow(panel), nrow(named),
      sum(!panel$is_marker & !grepl("^(FSC|SSC|Time)", panel$channel)),
      sum(grepl("^(FSC|SSC|Time)", panel$channel)),
      nrow(measures), length(unique(measures$alias_subject_id)),
      format(median(measures$total_events), big.mark = ",")
    )
  ),
  caption = "The deposit. The instrument is a four laser Cytek Aurora running SpectroFlo 2.2.0.2."
)
```

The panel carries 35 named markers and one unnamed channel, which is the
viability dye. That is 36 fluorescence parameters, and the paper describes itself
as 36 colour flow cytometry. The file and the sentence agree.

```{r}
#| label: markers

kable(
  data.frame(Marker = paste(named$marker, collapse = ", ")),
  caption = "Every named marker in the panel."
)
```

## Part 1: what spectral changes about the pipeline

Two steps of the conventional pipeline do not apply here, and one new step does.

Compensation does not apply. SpectroFlo unmixed the data before export, so the
files carry one column per fluorochrome and no spillover matrix. The keyword
`APPLY COMPENSATION` reads `FALSE` in all 83 files. The compensation work of the
OMIP-039 report has nothing to act on, and the pipeline starts at the transform.

The viability channel does not carry a marker name. `FluorescenceChannels()`
selects a channel only when `$PnS` is set, which is correct for a conventional
panel and wrong here, because the first gate of the hierarchy uses that channel.
`SpectralChannels()` keeps every channel that is not scatter and not time, and
the transform therefore covers the viability dye.

The new step is the cohort. This analysis compares 83 samples across 12
acquisition dates, so a gate that moves between samples moves the answer.

## Part 2: the cohort, and where the grouping comes from

The FCS files carry a subject code and a day. They carry no sex and no severity.
Table S1 of the paper carries both, and it keys on the same subject code that the
file name uses.

```{r}
#| label: cohort

design <- ReadOutput("cohort_design.csv")
kable(
  design,
  caption = "The cohort. Sampling was sex balanced by design, and a subject can appear at several time points.",
  col.names = c("Severity rank", "Sex", "Samples", "Subjects")
)
```

All 83 files match a metadata row, and the metadata marks exactly 83 samples as
included in the flow analysis. The join is therefore complete in both directions,
and `gating/yu2021_sample_metadata.csv` records it.

Read the subject column against the sample column. There are 83 samples and 45
subjects, so a subject contributes up to five samples. Every test below treats a
sample as independent. The paper appears to do the same. That inflates the
apparent precision, and the discussion returns to it.

## Part 3: one cut for the cohort, and the marker where that fails

An openCyto template fits every gate per sample. That is right when the question
is about one file. It is wrong here, because a cut that moves with the sample
changes a frequency for a reason that is not biology, and every claim in this
paper is a comparison between samples.

The cut points were therefore fitted once, on a pooled subsample of all 83 files,
and the same cut gates every sample.

```{r}
#| label: cuts

cuts <- ReadOutput("gate_cuts.csv")
kable(
  cuts[, c("marker", "parent", "side", "cut", "source")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Every cut point, on the logicle scale. The file gating/yu2021_gate_cuts.csv holds the reason for each one.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Parent", "Keep", "Cut", "Source")
)
```

Six of the seven marker cuts sit on a real minimum of the pooled density. CD3
has a minimum at 3.32, CD8 at 3.29, CCR7 at 3.23 and CD161 at 3.37, each of them
between two clear peaks.

CD45RA has no such minimum inside the CD8 gate. The only minima of its density
are at 0.08 and 0.74, which sit in the far negative tail where almost no events
are, and a gate placed there calls 94 percent of CD8 T cells positive. The
consequence is that the central memory and effector memory gates hold no events
at all.

The same reagent does resolve on CD4 T cells, where the density has a minimum at
2.54. That value is used for CD8 T cells as well. It is a choice, it is recorded
as a choice in the source column above, and Part 5 measures what the choice
changes.

```{r}
#| label: hierarchy

kable(
  ReadOutput("gating_hierarchy.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The hierarchy, as the median across the 83 samples.",
  col.names = c("Step", "Median", "Unit")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: failures

failures <- ReadOutput("gating_failures.csv")
cat(sprintf(
  "%d of %d files were gated. %d failed.\n",
  nrow(measures), nrow(measures) + nrow(failures), nrow(failures)
))
```

Two numbers say that the gates are in a sensible place. CD8 T cells are 32
percent of CD3 positive cells, which is the expected fraction in blood. CD161hi
cells are 9.1 percent of CD8 T cells, which is the range that the literature
reports for MAIT cells.

One number says that a gate is not. NK cells are 16.5 percent of CD45 positive
cells, which is about half of the CD3 negative parent, and B cells, monocytes and
dendritic cells also live there. The CD56 cut at 2.12 is too permissive. That gate
feeds claim 10 alone, which asks only whether NK cells carry more CD56 than CD8 T
cells, and a permissive gate makes that comparison harder rather than easier. No
other number in this report depends on it.

### What CD161hi is, and is not

The panel carries no Va7.2, so it cannot identify a MAIT cell by the invariant T
cell receptor. The paper reads MAIT cells as CD8 positive CD161hi T cells, and it
validates that surrogate with single cell RNA sequencing, where the CD161hi
cluster co-expresses `KLRB1`, `CD3D`, `CD8A` and `TRAV1-2`.

This report tests the flow claims only. It inherits the surrogate and it does not
check it.

## Part 4: the paper's claims against its own data

```{r}
#| label: group-medians

kable(
  ReadOutput("group_medians.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "CD161hi, memory and naive frequencies, as the median of each group.",
  col.names = c("Severity rank", "Sex", "Samples", "CD161hi percent",
                "Memory percent", "Naive percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: claims

kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "figure", "detail", "observed",
               "p_value", "verdict")],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Every claim the paper makes from the flow data, tested against the deposited files.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Figure", "Measured",
                "Direction found", "p", "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict-counts

kable(
  as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict)),
  caption = "How the ten claims came out.",
  col.names = c("Verdict", "Claims")
)
```

Nine of the ten claims reproduce. Read the direction column and the p column as
two different questions. The verdict compares the direction that was found
against the direction the paper states. The p value is the test the paper itself
used, which is Mann-Whitney for a two group comparison and Spearman for a
correlation. A direction can be right while the test is not significant, and
claims 2, 4 and 7 are exactly that. Claim 9 also sits above 0.05, but there the
absence of a difference is the claim itself.

### The headline claim

```{r}
#| label: severity-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD161hi cells against severity rank. The paper's Figure 1G and Figure 2B are the same comparison."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_by_severity.png"))
```

CD161hi cells fall as severity rises, with a Spearman rho of -0.236 and a p of
0.031 across 83 samples. That is the title of the paper's Figure 1.

The sex difference is larger than the severity difference. Healthy females carry
a median of 30.1 percent CD161hi cells among CD8 T cells and healthy males carry
6.3 percent. By the hospitalized group the two are 2.5 and 3.3 percent.

```{r}
#| label: slope-figure
#| fig-cap: "The regression of Figure 2C. The female slope is -5.07 percentage points per severity rank and the male slope is -1.31."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_slope_by_sex.png"))
```

The female slope is about four times the male slope. The paper writes that
females had a more dramatic loss of peripheral CD161hi cells compared with males,
and the deposited data says the same thing.

### The claim that does not reproduce

Claim 5 states that the greater abundance of CD161hi cells in females was lost at
early and middle time points but not in late disease. The data holds females
above males at all three time points, so the pattern the paper describes is not
there.

```{r}
#| label: timepoint-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD161hi cells by time after symptom onset. The paper reports that the female advantage disappears at early and middle."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_by_timepoint.png"))
```

The direction of the underlying difference is right in every window. What fails is
the interaction, which is the part of the claim that says the difference
disappears and comes back. That is the hardest kind of claim to reproduce,
because it needs three separate comparisons to fall out in a specific pattern,
and the smallest of those windows holds ten female samples.

```{r}
#| label: memory-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD8 memory cells by time after symptom onset. The male predominance holds in every window, which is claim 6."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("memory_by_timepoint.png"))
```

Claim 6 is the same shape of statement about the memory compartment, and it does
reproduce. Males sit above females at early, middle and late, with a p of 0.009.

## Part 5: what the CD45RA choice changes

Three of the ten claims are about the memory compartment, and the memory
compartment rests on the CD45RA cut, which Part 3 established is a choice rather
than a fit. The analysis therefore runs again at every cut from 2.4 to 4.2.

```{r}
#| label: sweep

kable(
  ReadOutput("cd45ra_sweep.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The three memory claims at every CD45RA cut. The file is read once and every cut is answered from the same events.",
  col.names = c("CD45RA cut", "Memory percent, median", "Naive percent, median",
                "Claim 4", "Claim 6", "Claim 8")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-figure
#| fig-cap: "The same table as a figure. No verdict changes anywhere in the range."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd45ra_sweep.png"))
```

The memory frequency moves from 55.5 to 65.3 percent across the range, which is
a large change in the number. No verdict changes.

That is the useful result. The cut point is not measurable from the data, and it
does not matter, because all three claims are comparisons between two groups
gated at the same place. A cut that is wrong by the same amount in both groups
cancels.

## Part 6: clustering as a second route

Sequential gating asks how many cells fall inside a boundary. Clustering asks how
many groups are in the data. The second question needs no hierarchy, so it is a
genuine second route to the same population.

```{r}
#| label: umap
#| fig-cap: "FlowSOM metaclusters on 249,000 live CD45+ events, drawn 3,000 per sample, which is the draw the paper used for its Figure 1B."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_metaclusters.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-markers
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by each lineage marker."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_markers.png"))
```

### Fifteen metaclusters on all leucocytes cannot find MAIT cells

The first attempt clustered every live CD45 positive event into 15 metaclusters
and looked for the CD161 high cluster among the CD8 T cell clusters. It selected
a metacluster of 484 events whose brightest marker was CD56, at a median of 4.41,
and whose CD161 median of 2.66 ranked fifth of the fifteen clusters. That is an
NK cell cluster and not a MAIT cluster.

The reason is the size of the population. CD161hi cells are 9 percent of CD8 T
cells, which is under 2 percent of the CD45 positive parent, and a rare
population is absorbed by a neighbouring metacluster when the number of
metaclusters is fixed in advance. The OMIP-039 report met the same failure on the
NK subsets.

### Clustering inside the CD8 gate does find them

```{r}
#| label: cd8-clusters

kable(
  ReadOutput("cd8_cluster_median_expression.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Ten metaclusters fitted inside the CD8 gate on 56,124 pooled events. Metacluster 9 carries a CD161 median of 3.76 against 2.46 in the runner up."
)
```

The margin is not a close call. The MAIT metacluster is chosen by the highest
median CD161 and no cluster is named by eye.

```{r}
#| label: route-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Every sample, gated and clustered. The dashed line is equality."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("route_comparison.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: clustering-claims

kable(
  ReadOutput("claim_verdicts_clustering.csv")[
    , c("claim_id", "short_name", "detail", "observed", "p_value", "verdict")
  ],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "The five CD161hi claims again, read from the metacluster instead of the gate.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Measured", "Direction found",
                "p", "Verdict")
)
```

The metacluster holds 9.14 percent of the pooled CD8 gate and the gate holds a
median of 9.13 percent. The two routes agree at a Spearman rho of 0.959 across
the 83 samples, having reached that number by different means. One fitted a
boundary on one marker. The other grouped events in eight dimensions and never
saw a gate.

Four of the five claims reproduce by both routes. Claim 5 comes out differently.
Under clustering the early window shows males above females, which is what the
paper describes, so the clustering route supports claim 5 in the window where the
gating route did not. Neither route produces the full pattern.

## Discussion

### What this shows

A published finding from a 35 marker spectral panel reproduces from the deposited
files, using an analysis that shares no code and no software with the original.
The authors used FlowJo and Omiq. This used flowCore, FlowSOM and one CSV of cut
points. Nine of ten claims come out with the direction the paper states, and the
central one comes out by two independent routes that agree at rho 0.959.

The claim that failed is an interaction rather than a difference, and it failed
in the direction of being too simple: females sit above males everywhere, instead
of only in late disease.

### Where the fragility sits

The OMIP-039 report ended by saying that a gate on a bimodal marker is robust and
a gate on a continuum is a decision. This dataset gives a cleaner example of the
same point, because it separates the two cases inside one panel.

CD3, CD8, CCR7 and CD161 are bimodal, their cuts were fitted from the pooled
density, and the analysis inherits nothing from the analyst at those four gates.
CD45RA is a continuum, its cut cannot be fitted, and the analysis inherits a
number that a person chose.

The sweep in Part 5 then shows that the chosen number changes the frequency by
ten percentage points and changes no conclusion. That is worth separating from
the general worry about gating. A cut point matters when the reported quantity is
a frequency. It cancels when the reported quantity is a comparison between two
groups gated at the same place.

### What this does not show

It does not show that the paper is right. It shows that the numbers in the paper
follow from the files the authors deposited. A shared error in the panel, in the
staining or in the cohort would survive this check untouched.

It does not test the MAIT surrogate. Every number here is CD161hi within CD8 T
cells, because the panel has no Va7.2, and whether that population is MAIT cells
rests on the sequencing in the paper.

The 83 samples come from 45 subjects, and every test treats a sample as
independent. A subject who contributes five samples counts five times. That
inflates the precision of every p value in Part 4, and it affects the claims
about time points most, because those windows are built from repeated sampling of
the same people. A mixed model with a subject random effect is the correct test
and it is not run here.

The normal group holds five females and five males. The largest effect in the
report, a median of 30.1 percent against 6.3 percent, rests on those ten samples.
The direction is clear and the magnitude is not settled by ten people.

### What is left to do

The dataset carries 12 acquisition dates between 29 May 2020 and 16 September
2020, and no batch correction was applied. CytoNorm is the tool for that and it
is not in the container, because it is on GitHub only and not on Bioconductor.
Adding it would test whether the severity correlation survives batch correction,
and that is the next check this analysis needs.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, not the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FlowRepository_FR-FCM-Z3WR_files

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/08_yu2021_spectral_mait.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/yu2021_spectral_mait.qmd
```

The clinical grouping comes from Table S1 of the paper. It is derived into
`gating/yu2021_sample_metadata.csv`, which is committed, so the join does not
depend on a download.

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
